passage: With ten minutes left before the picnic bus left, Kashish grabbed Sachin's cap and tossed it between two friends, and everyone laughed. He liked that sound; it made him feel tall. Sachin stood by the bus door and said nothing, his eyes on his shoes, his lip pressed white. For a moment Kashish really saw that look, and remembered his elder brother doing the same to him at home while the family watched. His laugh dried up. The teacher was calling out names and time was short, but Kashish walked over, held out the cap and said, "Sorry. That wasn't funny." Sachin took it without a word. It was not enough, and Kashish knew it.

qa.q: What did Kashish do with Sachin's cap?
qa.a: He tossed it between two friends.

qa.q: Why did Kashish's laugh dry up after he looked at Sachin?
qa.a: He saw the hurt in Sachin's face and it reminded him of how his elder brother treated him at home, so the teasing no longer made him feel big.

qa.q: What made Kashish's apology a step in the right direction, and what more might he do?
qa.a: He stopped, returned the cap and said sorry plainly; he could also stay kinder from now on and ask himself why he wanted to feel big.

qa.q: How might Sachin see the apology?
qa.a: Sachin took the cap without a word, so he may still feel hurt or unsure it is real; an apology starts repair but does not fix things at once.

grounding: A child who teases a quieter boy for laughs notices his hurt, stops and apologises.
